Abstract
Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) algorithms often require a large amount of data and
struggle in sparse-reward domains with long planning horizons and multiple sub-goals.
In this paper, we propose a neuro-symbolic extension of Proximal Policy Optimization
(PPO) that transfers partial logical policy specifications learned in easier instances to guide
learning in more challenging settings. We introduce two integrations of symbolic guidance:
(i) H-PPO-Product, which biases the action distribution at sampling time, and (ii) H-
PPO-SymLoss, which augments the PPO loss with a symbolic regularization term. We
evaluate our methods on three benchmarks (OfficeWorld, WaterWorld, and DoorKey),
showing consistently faster learning and higher return at convergence than PPO and a
Reward Machine baseline, also under imperfect symbolic knowledge.
1. Introduction
Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) (Sutton and Barto, 2018) is widely applied to solve
sequential decision-making problems.
It offers significant benefits for complex domains,
ranging from robotics (Ibarz et al., 2021) to sustainability (Zuccotto et al., 2024; K˚age
et al., 2025).
Despite these successes, scaling DRL to more challenging configurations
remains difficult. First, neural policies act as black boxes, limiting their interpretability
and making it hard to extract formal guarantees (Vouros, 2022). Furthermore, DRL suffers
from sample inefficiency (Dulac-Arnold et al., 2021). Agents often require a huge number of
interactions to converge to an optimal policy. This drawback becomes especially evident in
environments featuring long horizons, sparse rewards, and complex sequences of sub-goals.
Standard methods attempt to solve this by applying architectural inductive biases
(Wang et al., 2019) or by injecting domain knowledge through Reward Machines (RMs)
(Icarte et al., 2022). However, reliance on scalar reward shaping is often computationally
expensive and can degrade performance if the provided heuristics are inaccurate (Cheng
et al., 2021).
We propose a neuro-symbolic approach to improve the sample efficiency and scalability
of Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithms (Schulman et al., 2017). Our framework
uses logical policy representations as an action-level prior to guide PPO training in harder
configurations, where standard methods typically fail.

During training, an online reasoning mechanism translates the agent’s raw observations
into high-level logical predicates, capturing object states and spatial relationships. These
predicates are then evaluated against the previously extracted rules to deduce the most
promising actions at each step. We integrate these preferences into PPO via two distinct
methods: H-PPO-Product, which biases the learned policy towards the suggested actions,
hence modifying the action sampling distribution; and H-PPO-SymLoss, which adds a
symbolic penalty during optimization updates.
Our approach is designed to work with
imperfect logical rules (Hazra and De Raedt, 2023) and prevents the need to retune PPO
hyperparameters when the domain scale increases.
Our main contributions are the following:
• A sample-efficient neuro-symbolic PPO framework that leverages partial logical rules
to guide the agent toward logically entailed actions, employing either sampling distri-
bution biases or symbolic optimization penalties.
• An empirical validation on three well-established gridworld domains: OfficeWorld,
WaterWorld by Icarte et al. (2022), and DoorKey by Chevalier-Boisvert et al. (2023).
We show substantial improvements in sampling efficiency and return at convergence
over standard baselines and RMs, even in the hardest task instances and without
hyperparameter tuning.
2. Related Works
Sample inefficiency consistently restricts the scalability and applicability of algorithms like
PPO, particularly in sparse-reward environments with sub-goals and long planning horizons.
Traditional approaches to mitigate this issue remain purely neural, often improving data
efficiency by explicitly decoupling the training of the policy and the value function to enable
more aggressive sample reuse (Cobbe et al., 2021; Raileanu and Fergus, 2021). However,
these frameworks suffer from inherent opacity, lack a natural mechanism to directly integrate
human-readable domain rules and require careful tuning of the hyperparameters.
Neuro-symbolic integrations offer a way to combine logical reasoning with neural learning
to augment interpretability and generalization. Many methods translate formal task spec-
ifications into sequential automata, resulting in policy-correction mechanisms built from
trajectories (Yang et al., 2024) or automated reward shaping (De Giacomo et al., 2019;
Furelos-Blanco et al., 2021). Along this line, plan-based reward shaping and reward ma-
chines can still help when plans are incomplete or partly incorrect, using potential-based
signals to speed up learning in long-sequence sparse-reward tasks (M¨uller et al., 2025) or
guiding exploration (Icarte et al., 2022; Furelos-Blanco et al., 2021). Yet reward-based in-
terventions are highly sensitive to poorly-specified heuristics (Cheng et al., 2021), which has
pushed recent work toward mining logical rules directly from past trajectories (Meli et al.,
2024; Sreedharan and Katz, 2023; Veronese et al., 2024, 2025).
Our method builds upon the principle of semantic loss presented in Xu et al. (2018),
which encodes symbolic constraints over a neural network’s output as a differentiable
penalty. In our setting, we leverage the same general principle but target deep reinforcement
learning and policy-gradient optimization. We design a term defined through a symbolic
policy, composed of logical rules over predicates, and we study the role of a dedicated

methods share some similarities with Statistical Relational Learning (SRL) (Marra et al.,
2024) and the neuro-symbolic framework proposed in Hazra and De Raedt (2023). How-
ever, SRL and pure logical learning methods struggle to scale to complicated domains, as
they require an accurate definition of the policy search space. By combining the advantages
of symbolic reasoning and DRL, our approach overcomes the scalability bottlenecks of the
logic-driven policy learning proposed by Hazra and De Raedt (2023). As a result, our neuro-
symbolic agent can successfully navigate sparse-reward tasks involving extended sequences
of sub-goals, where standard DRL algorithms and purely symbolic methods typically fail.
Action-level guidance beyond reward modification is inspired from Veronese et al. (2026);
Meli et al. (2024); Sreedharan and Katz (2023), which however focused on model-based RL
or ϵ-greedy algorithms. Instead, our method is designed for the most advanced and popular
class of PPO algorithms for RL.

4. Methodology
Before describing our algorithms, we introduce the notion of action-level guidance.
In
contrast with the state heuristics adopted in classical planning (Bonet and Geffner, 2001),
we consider a logical preference over actions, which is more convenient for integration in RL
(Veronese et al., 2026; Meli et al., 2024). Specifically, the action-level guidance is provided
via a symbolic policy, expressed in a fragment of first-order logic (namely, Horn clauses).
Definition 1 (Symbolic Policy) Consider two sets of logical predicates F, A, represent-
ing abstractions for environmental (state) features and actions in RL, respectively. A sym-
bolic policy πsym : F →A is a set of logical rules over predicates that map environmental
features to action terms.
F, A are defined by the task designer. Formally, we follow classical works in symbolic and
neuro-symbolic AI (Coradeschi et al., 2013; Veronese et al., 2026; Sreedharan and Katz,
2023) and assume that there exist functions that map the MDP states and actions into sets
of grounded logical predicates: GF : S →G(F) and GA : A →G(A). We require GA to be
surjective, since we need each symbolic action to correspond to at least one MDP action.
The logical policy encodes rules in the form a ←f1, . . . , fn, where fi are environmental
predicates and a represents an action. For example, consider the DoorKey domain, where
an agent navigates a grid with walls, keys and doors; it must pick up the correct key and
open (toggle) the door to reach a goal location. In this setting πsym might contain logical
rules like:
toggle(X) ←door(X), locked(X), carryingKey(Z), sameColor(X, Z)
To integrate this symbolic knowledge into the RL loop, we define an indicator function
Iπsym : S × A →{0, 1}, such that:
Iπsym(s, a) = 1 ⇐⇒πsym(GF(s)) |= GA(a)
We now detail the two proposed neuro-symbolic integrations: H-PPO-Product and
H-PPO-SymLoss. Both methods leverage the logical guidance provided by Iπsym(s, a),
but they integrate this knowledge into PPO training differently.

5. Experiments
We evaluate our methodologies on three benchmarks2 (Figure 1): DoorKey from Chevalier-
Boisvert et al. (2023) and OfficeWorld and WaterWorld from Icarte et al. (2022). DoorKey
is a partially observable grid navigation task where the agent must retrieve a key that
matches the door color before reaching the final goal. OfficeWorld takes place in a discrete
grid containing labeled locations such as coffee, mail, plants, an office, and various rooms;
the agent must navigate through a sequence of sub-goals, while avoiding the plants. Wa-
terWorld is a continuous 2D box containing differently colored balls that move at constant
velocities and bounce off walls; the agent controls a white ball and must change its velocity
to touch specific color sequences in order, while avoiding out-of-sequence collisions. All
settings feature sparse rewards and (in some variants) long planning horizons, making them
suitable to test whether symbolic action preferences can improve exploration and policy
learning.
We compare against vanilla PPO and an RM baseline (Icarte et al., 2022).
In our
RM setup, rewards are shaped using (i) a small action-level bonus/penalty depending on
whether the chosen action is entailed by πsym, and (ii) additional rewards/penalties for
progressing or regressing along the states of the RM automaton equivalent to πsym. We
tune the main PPO hyperparameters only on the smallest domain instances, and keep them
fixed when moving to larger and more complex instances, except for the episode length and
the number of parallel environments to accommodate longer horizons. The hyperparameters
are reported in Appendix A.2.
Crucially, the symbolic policies are not perfect nor complete, but they are induced from
the agent’s experience in small and simple task instances and then transferred unchanged to
harder ones (see Appendix A.1). In particular, in DoorKey we induce the symbolic policy on
the smallest setting (8×8 with 1 key) and reuse it for all larger variants (8×8 with 2/4 keys
and 16 × 16 with 1/2/4 keys). In OfficeWorld, rules induced in DeliverCoffee are reused in
DeliverCoffeeAndMail, while PatrolABC uses its own policy including guidance for rooms
A, B, and C. In WaterWorld, we induce the symbolic policy on RedGreen and reuse the

5.1. DoorKey Results
Figure 2 reports the DoorKey results across varying grid sizes (8 × 8 and 16 × 16) and
number of keys (1, 2, 4). PPO hyperparameter tuning was performed in the 8×8 grid with
1 key.
In the 8×8 grid (top row), we observe consistent gains from both H-PPO-Product and
H-PPO-SymLoss across all key configurations. With 1 key, all methods converge rapidly,
though RMs have more variable performance. However, as the number of keys increases,
our algorithms become increasingly beneficial.
In particular, H-PPO-Product clearly
demonstrates its strength in driving exploration, reaching high return with faster growth
in the earliest episodes. Meanwhile, H-PPO-SymLoss reaches the same high return, but
more slowly. Interestingly, in the 4-key settings the RM baseline remains at zero return
throughout training, so its curve lies on the horizontal axis and is barely visible in the
charts, making it the weakest performer.
Scaling to the 16 × 16 grid shows the crucial role of exploration, with a longer plan-
ning horizon. Indeed, H-PPO-Product is the only algorithm reaching near-optimal per-
formance even in the most challenging setting with 4 keys, having the longest planning
horizon.

5.2. OfficeWorld Results
Figure 3 reports the OfficeWorld results for DeliverCoffee, PatrolAB, DeliverCoffeeAndMail
and PatrolABC.
In the simpler tasks DeliverCoffee and PatrolAB, H-PPO-Product exhibits the fastest
rise and reaches near-optimal return early, while PPO and the RM baseline follow closely;
H-PPO-SymLoss lags in the first phase but catches up later, ending slightly below the top
curves. In PatrolAB, the same pattern holds: H-PPO-Product leads the early learning,
whereas H-PPO-SymLoss steadily improves and attains the best return at convergence.
Moving to the harder DeliverCoffeeAndMail and PatrolABC tasks, H-PPO-Product
achieves the fastest initial learning due to its exploration bias, but its average return
plateaus at a lower level (slightly above 0.65 in DeliverCoffeeAndMail). In contrast, H-
PPO-SymLoss improves more slowly at the start (as it provides less exploration pull),
but its symbolic regularization strongly shapes the final policy, reaching the highest re-
turns in both tasks. The RM baseline shows moderate performance but remains below
H-PPO-SymLoss. These results demonstrate that H-PPO-SymLoss is highly effective at
maximizing policy returns, but does not yield a good initial exploration.

In the RedGreen task (where PPO hyperparameters were tuned), all methods easily
learn the optimal behavior. However, as the tasks become more complex, the differences
in performance become clear. In RedGreenAndBlueCyan, H-PPO-Product emerges as
the most robust approach, actively driving the exploration toward trajectories that follow
the required ordering and reaching the highest return close to 0.6. The RM baseline also
performs better than standard PPO. At the same time, H-PPO-SymLoss struggles more
than standard PPO, as modifying the policy loss early in training may overly constrain the
exploration dynamics.
In the hardest task (RedGreenAndBlueCyanAndMagentaYellow), these differences are
amplified. As the required sequences become longer, only H-PPO-Product successfully
achieves the required exploration to reach higher returns. H-PPO-SymLoss is not effective
here, confirming that its primary strength lies in policy consolidation after successes are
encountered naturally, rather than in initiating complex exploration sequences out of sparse-
reward spaces.
6. Conclusion
In this paper, we proposed a neuro-symbolic framework for improving the sample efficiency
of PPO in environments characterized by sparse rewards, multiple sub-goals, and long plan-
ning horizons. Our two integration strategies, H-PPO-Product and H-PPO-SymLoss,
inject logical rules into the learning process at the level of action selection and policy opti-
mization, respectively, while progressively annealing their influence so that training recovers
standard PPO, without hyperparameter re-tuning when scaling to harder instances.
Across three benchmark environments and multiple variants, our methods consistently
outperform the baselines, including state-of-the-art reward machines, fulfilling distinct roles.
H-PPO-Product proves to be an exploration driver, achieving the fastest convergence and
highest final returns in the long, sparse spaces of DoorKey and WaterWorld. Conversely, H-
PPO-SymLoss does not significantly aid in early exploration, but acts as a powerful prior
for policy regularization; this is clear in OfficeWorld, where it results in the highest returns
despite slower initial exploration. Taken together, these results demonstrate that integrating
symbolic reasoning directly into the algorithmic structure of DRL offers an effective path
towards interpretable, and sample-efficient policy learning and generalization.
Future work will investigate extensions to continuous action spaces, more challenging
domains, and the potential for zero-shot generalization in DRL, towards actual real-world
application.

Appendix A.
A.1. Domains
A.1.1. DoorKey
DoorKey is a partially observable grid navigation task (Figure 1(a)) where the agent (red
arrow) must retrieve a key, unlock a door of the same color, and then reach the goal cell
(green).
The MDP observation covers a 7 × 7 area (light gray), with each cell encoded by object
type, color and state. The discrete action set has five actions: turn left, turn right,
move forward, pick up and toggle (used to open the door).
Rewards are sparse: the agent is rewarded only when it reaches the goal after opening
the required door. In that case the reward is r(s, a) = 1 −0.9 · step count
max steps , with max steps =
env size · env size · 10 as defined by the environment, otherwise the reward is zero.
The symbolic policy contains the logical rules from Hazra and De Raedt (2023):
1. pickup(X) ←key(X), sameColor(X, Y), door(Y), notCarrying
2. toggle(X) ←door(X), locked(X), carryingKey(Z), sameColor(X,Z)
3. goto(X) ←goal(X), unlocked
Rule 1 recommends picking up a key X when it matches the color of a door Y and the agent
is not already carrying a key. Rule 2 suggests unlocking a door X when the agent holds
a key Z with the same color and the door is locked. Rule 3 then directs the agent toward
the goal X once the door is unlocked. Unlike the first two, this rule is not tied to a single
low-level action and is treated as a high-level navigation directive.
A.1.2. OfficeWorld
OfficeWorld (Figure 1(b)) is a grid environment with a rectangular layout and static labeled
locations such as mail (m), coffee (c), office (o) and decorative plants (∗) that serve as
obstacles. Extra rooms labeled A through D appear depending on the task variant. The
agent (red arrow) moves deterministically with four actions: up, down, left, right.
The observation space includes the agent’s grid position, whether it is holding coffee,
whether it is holding mail, and the progress through room visitation. Rewards are sparse
and given only at goal completion: r(s, a) = 1−0.9· step count
max steps , with max steps = env width·
env height · 10 by default, otherwise the reward is zero.
We consider four variants of the general task:
• DeliverCoffeeAndMail, where the agent must collect both coffee and mail before reach-
ing the office. We use the following rules from Furelos-Blanco et al. (2021):
1. goto(X) ←coffee(X), not HasCoffee, notHittingPlants
2. goto(X) ←office(X), HasCoffee, notHittingPlants
These rules cover only the deliver coffee subtask.

• DeliverCoffee, a simplified variant where the agent only needs to collect the coffee and
then reach the office. It uses the same rules as DeliverCoffeeAndMail.
• PatrolABC, where the agent must visit rooms A, B and C in order while avoiding
plants. The corresponding rules by Furelos-Blanco et al. (2021) are:
1. goto(X) ←room a(X), not visited a, not visited b
not visited c, notHittingPlants
2. goto(X) ←room b(X), visited a, not visited b
not visited c, notHittingPlants
3. goto(X) ←room c(X), visited a, visited b,
not visited c, notHittingPlants
• PatrolAB, which only requires visiting rooms A and B in order while avoiding plants.
The symbolic policy follows the same structure as PatrolABC, but includes only the
rules for rooms A and B.
A.1.3. WaterWorld
WaterWorld (Figure 1(c)) is a continuous 2D box populated by moving colored balls that
bounce off the walls. The agent controls a white ball by changing its velocity with five
actions: up, down, left, right, and none. At every step, the observation is the set of
colors currently colliding with the agent, and the task is to touch balls in a prescribed color
sequence. Rewards are sparse: the agent receives r(s, a) = 1 −0.9 · step count
max steps only when the
sequence(s) are completed, otherwise zero, with max steps = env size/2 by default.
We evaluate three variants where multiple sequences can be interleaved. The logical
rules are simple progression constraints over the color-touch events:
• RedGreen:
1. touch(red) ←not touched red, not touched green.
2. touch(green) ←touched red, not touched green.
The first rule recommends seeking a red collision until it happens; the second switches
to green once red has been touched. They are both not actually tied to a single low-
level action and are treated as high-level navigation directives.
• RedGreenAndBlueCyan and RedGreenAndBlueCyanAndMagentaYellow: the symbolic
policy is the same as RedGreen; the blue→cyan and magenta→yellow sequences are
unsuggested.

A.3. Ablation Study for Θ in H-PPO-SymLoss
We investigated two regimes for Θ in H-PPO-SymLoss:
• a linearly decaying schedule Θt = max(Θi −t · Θr, Θf) with Θi = 1, Θf = 0 and
Θr = 0.4 (standard H-PPO-SymLoss in the main paper);
• fixed constant weights Θ ∈{0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0}.
Across all domains, our results demonstrate that maintaining a high, constant symbolic
penalty often suppresses the necessary initial exploration, leading to suboptimal conver-
gence.
On the other hand, lower constant weights allow for more exploration but offer
weaker eventual regularization. The decaying Θt schedule consistently achieves the best
balance, successfully combining early exploration with strong subsequent policy stabiliza-
tion. The results are reported in Figures 5, 6, 7.

A.4. Ablation Study for εf in H-PPO-Product
We study the effect of the symbolic influence in H-PPO-Product by fixing εf while
keeping the linear decay schedule unchanged, i.e., εt = max(εi −t · εr, εf) with εi = 0 and
εr = 0.4. In particular, we compare three constant terminal values:
• εf = 0 (standard H-PPO-Product in the main paper);
• εf = 0.2;
• εf = 0.4.
Overall, the impact is modest on easier instances, where all curves quickly reach similar
returns (e.g., DoorKey 8 × 8 with 1 key and WaterWorld RedGreen). As the tasks become
harder, maintaining a small symbolic bias is helpful: εf = 0.2 and εf = 0.4 tend to improve
stability and final performance in the largest DoorKey grids, OfficeWorld PatrolABC, and
the hardest WaterWorld sequence, while leaving the learning speed mostly unchanged. We
observe a mild trade-off in the easiest OfficeWorld task (DeliverCoffee), where larger εf
can slightly reduce the final return, suggesting that a nonzero εf is most beneficial in long-
horizon, sparse-reward regimes. Given that these differences are limited in most tasks, we
keep εf = 0 in Section 5. The results are reported in Figures 8, 9, 10.

Abstract: Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) algorithms often require a large amount of data and struggle in sparse-reward domains with long planning horizons and multiple sub-goals. In this paper, we propose a neuro-symbolic extension of Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) that transfers partial logical policy specifications learned in easier instances to guide learning in more challenging settings. We introduce two integrations of symbolic guidance: (i) H-PPO-Product, which biases the action distribution at sampling time, and (ii) H- PPO-SymLoss, which augments the PPO loss with a symbolic regularization term. We evaluate our methods on three benchmarks (OfficeWorld, WaterWorld, and DoorKey), showing consistently faster learning and higher return at convergence than PPO and a Reward Machine baseline, also under imperfect symbolic knowledge.
